summary:
Honduran law does not criminalise gender identity, and same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1899 with the age of consent set at 15 years for both same-sex and heterosexual conduct.

The Penal Code adopted by Decree No. 23-2013 and in force since March 2017 treats hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating circumstance in criminal responsibility under Article 27. Article 321 punishes anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies individual or collective rights, or refuses a professional service, on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages. Article 321-A punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred, contempt, persecution, violence or attacks on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of L.50,000 to L.300,000. LGBTQ rights groups met with Congress before the new code took effect to press for clear wording, and the anti-discrimination articles were retained.

The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs allows police to arrest anyone who "goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals". LGBTQ rights organisations have documented numerous instances of police using that provision as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space.

Human Rights Watch reported in May 2009 on police rape, assault and extortion of transgender people in Honduras. The Law Education Fund report "Left in the Dark" finds that transgender women in particular face major obstacles to justice, and attributes the resulting impunity to under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources and intentional case mishandling; the report concludes that institutions fail to effectively investigate and prosecute these cases.

Transgender women are held within the men's prison system. A 2017 account drawing on the torture-prevention centre CPTRT records that at Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the "La Isla" module beside the mentally-ill unit, that trans women are forced to cut their hair and barred from presenting as women, and that conjugal visits are denied. At Penitenciaria de Marcala, authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after CPTRT intervention was she isolated from the men and her feminine belongings returned. In 2020 a Honduran judge told Human Rights Watch of a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards; the judge said she had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate, and stated that there is no way to protect trans women in men's prisons.

Documented killings include transgender activist Cynthia Nicole, shot dead on 2 January, and trans activist Thalia Rodriguez, killed on 10 January 2022 in Tegucigalpa. No later killing is documented in the sources cited here. Sources also tally 174 violent deaths of LGBTQ people from 2009 to 2014, of which 69 were transgender, and 264 LGBTQ people murdered between 2009 and 2017; these are raw counts carrying no population or general-homicide denominator, so they do not establish a trans-specific rate.

Marriage and de facto union between persons of the same sex are prohibited. Decree 36 of 4 May 2005 amended Constitution Article 112 to restrict marriage to a man and a woman who have that status naturally and to refuse recognition of same-sex marriages or unions performed legally abroad; Article 116 prohibits adoption by same-sex couples. Same-sex couples and same-sex-headed households are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. Following the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018, activists filed suit with the Supreme Court in May 2018 to legalise same-sex marriage, a second case was dismissed in November 2018 for technical errors, and a same-sex marriage bill was presented to the National Congress on 24 May 2022 and remained under discussion.

The case of Vicky Hernández v Honduras, heard at the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case. Human Rights Watch finds that Central American states exclude transgender women from femicide legal frameworks, with officials in one neighbouring jurisdiction describing them as "not biological women".
tangentialFactors:
Political hostility toward LGBTQ rights is on record. The two major parties have mostly ignored LGBTQ rights, only a handful of dissident members of the Democratic Unification Party expressed interest in working with the LGBT community, and three candidates who backed same-sex marriage before the November 2017 elections all failed to win National Congress seats. President Juan Orlando Hernández said on 12 October 2018 that personally as a Christian he is against same-sex marriage, and the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association urged President Xiomara Castro to stop "immoral laws".

Transgender political visibility has carried security costs. A trans activist and co-founder of Asociación Cozumel Trans ran for Congress in Francisco Morazán for the PINU party at the 26 November 2017 election, receiving 11,112 votes and placing 136th in a race for 128 seats, an unsuccessful bid that was potentially the first openly trans candidacy. Context includes Kendra Stefani Jordany's 2017 primary win, Claudia Spellman's 2012 run for the LIBRE party, and Victoria Gomez seeking asylum in Spain after threats and attacks in Tegucigalpa. In June 2013 a trans woman was granted asylum in Spain after a police officer attempted to assassinate her.

The US State Department's 2021 Human Rights Report for Honduras lists violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons among significant human-rights issues, alongside extrajudicial killings, torture, corruption and lack of accountability for gender-based violence.

The GlobalGayz Honduras archive carries a dated index of LGBT news from 2004 to 2011, including an August 2004 church protest at state recognition of three gay groups, 2009-10 items on an LGBT activist murdered amid violence and impunity, extreme violence against the gay community and post-coup abuses, and 2005 coverage of marriage and adoption bans. These dated items corroborate the violence timeline for Honduras.

Public organising continues under conservative pressure. About 400 people marched in a pride parade in July 2017 in San Pedro Sula, and in 2004 the government extended formal recognition to three LGBTQ rights interest groups despite organised protests from the Catholic Church, Pentecostals and conservative legislators.
localsOnly:
A name change for LGBTI persons is approved in Honduras; no procedure details are given in the sources, and the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association described the practice as an "aberration in God's eyes".

Residents in same-sex relationships receive none of the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples, and same-sex couples are barred from adoption under Article 116 of the Constitution.

Early LGBTQ organisations faced structural barriers: initial efforts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met government opposition or extended delays, the first organisations arose often in response to the HIV/AIDS pandemic, held no legal standing and were essentially ignored by the government apart from police harassment.

The government offers medical care to all citizens and has worked increasingly with non-governmental organisations on HIV/AIDS awareness, but the socially conservative influence of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestants has made it difficult to implement any comprehensive public programme. Female prostitutes and men who have sex with men are identified as the highest-risk groups, and no youth-specific care or medication provisions appear in the sources.

Transgender political participation has produced candidacies at national level in 2012 and 2017, including a primary win in 2017, without resulting in elected office.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses entry or visa rules, passport or identity-document gender markers, legal gender recognition procedures, or airport screening treatment of transgender travellers. Those questions remain unresolved here.

The Reuters feature on Central America's LGBT people returning HTTP 401 was not retrievable at research time, so its claims are not carried.

The name change process for LGBTI persons is stated as available but no procedure, timeline or documentation requirement is sourced.

The killing tallies for 2009-2014 and 2009-2017 are raw counts without population or general-homicide denominators, and the sources provide no per-capita comparison, so they cannot be read as a trans-specific rate or used to rank risk.

The sources document no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically; the only general social-conditions statement available is that there is a social environment of historical discrimination against LGBTQ persons motivated by prejudice and machismo.

The date of Cynthia Nicole's killing is given as 2 January without a year in the source text, while Thalia Rodriguez's killing is dated 10 January 2022; the year of the first killing is not resolved here.
